question:
Patient note:
A 58-year-old man arrived to the urgent musculoskeletal clinic late this morning reporting that his right lower leg had become “tight like a sausage” over the past day and a half, causing him to loosen the straps of his walking boot and prop the extremity on a stack of pillows at night. Nine days earlier he sustained a nondisplaced Weber A fibular fracture after slipping off a curb; in the emergency department at that time a posterior splint was applied, and two days later an orthopedic office visit converted the splint to a molded, circumferential below-knee plaster cast that extends from just distal to the tibial tuberosity to the metatarsal heads with the ankle held at neutral. He has remained otherwise active—he hops short distances on the contralateral leg using crutches, prepares his own meals in the kitchen, and sleeps in an upstairs bedroom—so he has not been confined to bed for any prolonged interval. His past history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1 000 mg twice daily, mild hyperlipidemia treated with atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and seasonal allergic rhinitis; he has never had a blood clot, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, stroke, malignancy, or surgery, and there is no family history of thrombophilia. He denies tobacco; he drinks two cans of light beer on weekends and does not use illicit substances. Current medications are limited to metformin, atorvastatin, and as-needed acetaminophen; he takes no estrogen, testosterone, glucocorticoids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or anticoagulants. Since the cast was placed he has adhered to the surgeon’s advice to keep the leg elevated when seated, but beginning yesterday morning he noted diffuse fullness in the posterior calf that did not abate with rest and by last evening an imprint from the edge of his sock lingered several minutes. He denies new trauma to the limb, fevers, rigors, sweats, skin abrasions, insect bites, rash, focal redness, groin mass, chest discomfort, dyspnea, cough, palpitations, abdominal pain, flank pain, dysuria, or unintended weight change. In triage—before any analgesic, fluid, or antithrombotic administration—vital signs were temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg, heart rate 90 beats min⁻¹ regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air; he sat comfortably in a chair with the right leg resting on a stool, the cast split along its lateral aspect by staff for inspection but still otherwise intact. Cardiopulmonary examination revealed a crisp S₁ and S₂ without murmurs or gallops and clear lung fields throughout. Abdomen was soft, nontender, and without organomegaly; there were no jugular vein distention or peripheral edema elsewhere. Inspection of the lower extremities showed the casted limb to be noticeably fuller at mid-calf compared with the uninjured side; after the stockinette and padding were peeled back nurses used a cloth tape to measure 44.6 cm at a point exactly 10 cm below the inferior pole of the patella versus 40.2 cm on the left, a discrepancy of 4.4 cm. Fifteen centimeters above the patella both thighs measured 55.1 cm, and ankle girths at the malleoli were 29.3 cm on the right (inclusive of minimal cast padding) versus 28.7 cm on the left. Thumb pressure over the anteromedial tibial border of the symptomatic calf created a 4-mm depression that persisted approximately twenty seconds before rebounding; identical pressure on the contralateral leg rebounded immediately. The overlying skin beneath the cast appeared uniformly pink, was neither warmer nor cooler than the examiner’s hand, and displayed no serpiginous dilated channels, varicosities, ulcers, or brawny discoloration. Palpation was limited by the recent injury, yet gentle compression along the gastrocnemius and soleus bellies elicited only a diffuse sense of tightness without discrete cords or nodularity; range of motion at the knee was full, while ankle motion was restricted by the cast. Distal pulses—dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial—were palpable at 2 + bilaterally, capillary refill to all toes was under two seconds, protective sensation was intact to light touch, and motor strength of the contralateral limb remained 5/5. No inguinal or popliteal adenopathy was appreciated. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained before phlebotomy demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 88 beats min⁻¹ with no ST-T changes. Baseline laboratory tests drawn prior to any therapy revealed hemoglobin 13.8 g dL⁻¹, white blood cells 7.2 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, platelet count 247 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 138 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.2 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 12 mg dL⁻¹, creatinine 0.96 mg dL⁻¹, alanine aminotransferase 22 U L⁻¹, aspartate aminotransferase 19 U L⁻¹, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 27 s. Plain radiographs obtained immediately after cast splitting showed the original fracture alignment unchanged and no new osseous lesion or soft-tissue gas. Clinical examination disclosed unilateral calf enlargement exceeding 3 cm accompanied by grade 1 pitting confined to the immobilized limb in a patient who has remained ambulatory and possesses no prior thrombotic history, systemic edema, or inflammatory signs to suggest another clear etiology; comprehensive venous duplex ultrasonography from the common femoral segment to infrapopliteal veins was therefore requested on an expedited basis while he awaits imaging in observation, hemodynamically stable, and before initiation of any anticoagulant therapy.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Wells DVT score adds 1 point for each positive risk factor or examination finding and subtracts 2 if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT.
1. Recent plaster immobilization of the symptomatic leg: +1.
2. Calf enlargement ≥3 cm: 44.6 − 40.2 = 4.4 cm, so +1.
3. Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg: +1.
4. No active cancer, previous DVT, or qualifying bed rest or recent major surgery: 0 each. He remains mobile on crutches.
5. Diffuse tightness without localized deep venous tenderness, calf rather than whole-leg swelling, and no collateral superficial veins: 0 each.
6. No alternative diagnosis is judged at least as likely as DVT: 0 rather than −2.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.
Final answer: 3
